archetype.name: Game Manager (run-first leash)
archetype.definition: A second-year former No. 1 pick being asked to work underneath in the league's most run-heavy offense, protecting the ball and moving the chains rather than pushing it downfield.

report.headline: Cleaner and more accurate, but the leash is too short to matter yet
report.take:
Cam Ward's second season looks like a deliberate reset. The Titans pass 10.5 points less often than game situations predict in neutral states, the lowest rate in the league, and Ward's own throwing profile has shrunk with it. His aggressiveness (throws into tight windows) is down from 12.6% as a rookie to 7.56%, his intended air yards sit at 6.49, and the average throw lands 2.73 yards short of the sticks. This is a quarterback being kept in a box, and in some ways it is working. His CPOE has swung from -2.93 last year to +3.41 (16th of 42), his bad-throw rate is down from 17.6% to 15.1%, and his pressure-to-sack rate has dropped from 32.2% to 23.8%. He holds the ball about as long as he did as a rookie (2.94 seconds vs 3.0), but he is getting rid of it instead of taking the sack.

The problem is that tidier play hasn't produced better results. His EPA per dropback is -0.108, barely better than last year's -0.124, and the team is 0-4. The depth splits show why. The conservative part of the menu is what's losing. Throws behind the line are at -0.358 EPA on 18 attempts with a 22% success rate, and short throws are at -0.177 and hold both of his interceptions. The one area that works is the one the scheme uses least. On 25 throws at 10-19 yards he is at +0.579 EPA with a 12.4 CPOE. The deep ball is close to non-existent, with 2 completions on 10 attempts. An offense that throws short on early downs keeps leaving him in third-and-long. He has faced an average of 8.6 yards to go on third down and converted 26.5%.

The overall line also flatters him in one way and hurts him in another. When trailing by nine or more he is roughly average (+0.055, 8.4 CPOE, all three passing TDs). In one-score games, where the play-calling is tightest, he is at -0.284 with both interceptions. Some of the 'improvement' is soft-coverage production. His rushing has been worth +0.458 EPA per carry, and scrambles have turned 10 dropbacks into four first downs. But his two rushing TDs came in one game on a total of 13 carries, so that is not a scoring source to count on.

The best two passing games came as heavy underdogs. Against PHI (+7) and BAL (+11.5) the staff opened it up a bit: aggressiveness 9.7% and 7.1 intended air yards at Baltimore, and CPOE above 6 in both. That is the case for more trust. The case against arrives now. Both guards in the rotation, Fernando Carmona (67% of snaps) and Jackson Slater (33%), are on IR until about November 1. Interior protection had been a quiet strength, with the line's hit rate ranking 6th and Ward pressured on only 16.9% of dropbacks.

strengths.title: Accuracy jump from rookie year
strengths.body: His completion rate over expected went from below average to above average, and his bad-throw rate fell by about two and a half points. Some of that comes from easier throws in a short-area scheme. But his intermediate accuracy (12.4 CPOE at 10-19 yards) says the ball placement itself has improved, not just the menu. A one-year change backed by a lower bad-throw rate is more likely real than noise, though the charting still ranks his bad-throw rate in the bottom third.

strengths.title: Intermediate middle-depth passing
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 yards are his only efficient area: +0.579 EPA and a 56% success rate. This is where his arm and improved timing show up, and it is the clearest argument for the staff to loosen the restrictions. It is only 25 attempts, so the exact number will come down, but the gap to everything else is too large to be all luck.

strengths.title: Taking fewer sacks, scrambling usefully
strengths.body: His pressure-to-sack rate dropped from 32.2% to 23.8%, and when he does leave the pocket it pays: four first downs on 10 scrambles at +0.261 EPA per scramble. He hasn't lost a fumble. This is the most sustainable part of his growth because it is a decision-making habit rather than a hot split.

concerns.title: The safe throws are losing plays
concerns.body: Screens and short throws make up 84 of his 119 attempts, and both buckets have negative EPA, with both interceptions coming short. Some of this is the scheme's fault. Throws behind the line with a 22% success rate point to blocking and design as much as the quarterback. Either way, it guarantees long third downs, and he faces an average of 8.6 yards to go. Unless the staff shifts the mix toward the intermediate game, this stays.

concerns.title: No functional deep game
concerns.body: Two completions on 10 deep attempts, at -20.5 CPOE, and aggressiveness down from 12.6% to 7.56%. The small sample means the completion rate will rise. But the low volume is a choice, and an offense with no vertical threat lets defenses squeeze the short area where he already struggles.

concerns.title: Interior line losses arrive
concerns.body: Losing both rotation guards to IR removes a part of the offense that had been working: pressure on only 16.9% of dropbacks and a 6th-ranked hit rate allowed. Ward still holds the ball close to three seconds, so any added interior pressure turns into sacks or rushed throws. This lasts until roughly November 1.

trend.note: His passing EPA by game alternates: -7.4, -0.1, -6.5, +0.4. The two near-neutral outings came as big underdogs when the passing game was opened up, including his most aggressive, deepest-throwing game at Baltimore.

nextGame.headline: A leaky secondary, but a pass rush aimed at weakened guards
nextGame.body:
Houston's defense is an odd fit for Ward. Overall it ranks 25th in EPA and 25th against the pass, allows the 3rd-highest explosive pass rate (29th) and ranks 29th against deep throws. The catch is that those are the explosive plays Ward rarely creates. Down to down, the Texans are stingy: 4th in success rate allowed and 2nd in sack rate. A quarterback who throws short and holds the ball close to three seconds is playing into what they do well. QBs have averaged 286.3 yards and 19.5 PPR points against them (26th), so the ceiling is there if Tennessee lets him attack it.

Availability tilts things both ways. Houston is without LB Azeez Al-Shaair (92% of snaps), and Kenneth Murray Jr. (82%) is questionable after a concussion evaluation. That thins the second level exactly where Ward has struggled (-0.476 EPA on throws to the middle) and where his intermediate strength lives. On his side, Tennessee is now without both rotation guards, which is the worst possible timing against the league's No. 2 sack-rate defense.

keyMatchups.title: Texans' rush vs. replacement guards
keyMatchups.body: Houston sacks quarterbacks on 8.7% of dropbacks, and Tennessee is down Carmona and Slater inside. Ward has cut his sack rate by getting the ball out under pressure. This is the toughest test of that habit so far, and interior pressure gives him nowhere to step up.

keyMatchups.title: Middle of the field without Al-Shaair
keyMatchups.body: Ward has been poor working the middle (47.1% completions, -17.7 CPOE), but he has been strong at intermediate depth. With Houston's top linebacker out and the next one questionable, in-breaking routes at 10-19 yards are the cleanest path to efficiency.

keyMatchups.title: Underdog script opens the playbook
keyMatchups.body: As 7-point home dogs, the Titans could be throwing from behind. That has been his most productive state: +0.055 EPA and all three passing TDs when trailing by 9+. Houston's 30th-ranked rushing offense makes it less likely they can sit on a lead.

nextGame.watch: Whether Tennessee calls more 10-19-yard throws early, before the game script forces it, or keeps living on screens that are already losing behind a depleted interior line.

restOfSeason.body:
What should last: the accuracy gains, the lower sack rate and the useful scrambling. Those reflect real habits that improved from last year. What should regress: two rushing TDs on 13 carries, and a red-zone line with 3 TDs on 35.7% completions. His deep completion rate should climb off 20% simply on volume. His intermediate EPA will fall off the current +0.579 on 25 throws.

The bigger issue is volume and design. In the league's least pass-happy offense, his yardage stays modest unless games turn into chases, and with this defense (26th against the pass) they often will. Expect roughly 180-220 yards a week with more of it in the second half of losses. The next month, with both guards out, is the riskiest stretch for sacks and turnovers. The guards' return around November and any loosening of the play-calling are the upside paths.
swingFactors: Whether the staff raises his early-down pass rate and intermediate volume
Interior pass protection until the guards return around Nov. 1
How often Tennessee's 26th-ranked pass defense puts him in catch-up mode

bets.reason: Tennessee has covered both games as a big underdog (+7 vs PHI, +11.5 at BAL), and its run-first approach shortens games. Houston's 30th-ranked rushing offense is poorly built to pull away. Seven points is a lot in a 39.5 total.

Houston allows 286.3 yards a game to quarterbacks (26th) and the 3rd-highest explosive pass rate. It is missing its top linebacker, and Tennessee's 7-point underdog spot points to a pass-heavier script. The 2nd-ranked sack rate against two backup guards is the real risk, which keeps this a lean.
Both of his rushing TDs came in one game, and he has only 3 designed runs all season. It is a tiny, non-repeatable sample that shouldn't price him as a goal-line runner.

confidence.note: Four games and 119 attempts; the year-over-year accuracy change is supported, but the depth splits are small and the line just lost two guards.
